The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions. It repeatedly performs the
fetch-decode-execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it
means, and execute it. CPU speed is measured in gigahertz (GHz), billions of cycles
per second. Modern CPUs contain multiple cores, each capable of executing instructions
independently, which allows a computer to make progress on several tasks at once.

Computers use a hierarchy of storage that trades speed against capacity and cost.
Registers inside the CPU are the fastest and smallest. Cache memory sits next to the
CPU cores and holds recently used data. Random access memory (RAM) is the computer's
working memory: it holds running programs and their data, and its contents are lost
when power is removed — RAM is volatile. Persistent storage — solid-state drives (SSD)
and hard disk drives (HDD) — retains data without power. SSDs use flash memory with no
moving parts and are much faster than HDDs, which store data on spinning magnetic
platters.

The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects every component. Buses are the
communication pathways that carry data between the CPU, memory, and devices. The
chipset manages traffic between components. Expansion slots allow additional cards,
such as a dedicated graphics card, to be added.

Input devices bring data into the computer: keyboards, mice, touchscreens, cameras,
and microphones. Output devices present results: monitors, speakers, and printers.
Ports such as USB provide standardized connections for peripherals. Device drivers are
software components that let the operating system communicate with specific hardware.

The graphics processing unit (GPU) contains thousands of small cores designed to
perform many simple calculations simultaneously. GPUs were created to render images
and video, but their parallel design also makes them well suited to scientific
computing and training machine learning models.

In 1965, Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip doubled
roughly every two years, an observation known as Moore's law. For decades this drove
exponential growth in computing power at falling cost. In recent years the pace has
slowed as transistors approach physical limits, pushing the industry toward multi-core
designs, specialized chips, and better software efficiency.

retrieved_chunks:
An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. A recipe is a
useful analogy: given ingredients (input), following the steps produces a dish
(output). For a procedure to be an algorithm, its steps must be unambiguous, it must
finish after a finite number of steps, and it must produce a correct result for every
valid input. The same algorithm can be expressed in English, in pseudocode, or in any
programming language.

Pseudocode describes an algorithm in structured, language-neutral text. It uses
constructs such as IF/ELSE for decisions, WHILE and FOR for repetition, and variables
for storing values, without the exact syntax of any programming language. Pseudocode
lets people design and discuss an algorithm before writing real code.

Linear search finds a target value in a list by checking each element one at a time,
from the first to the last, until the target is found or the list is exhausted. In the
worst case, linear search examines every element. Its advantage is simplicity: it
works on any list, sorted or not.

Binary search finds a target value in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search
range. It compares the target to the middle element: if the target is smaller, the
search continues in the left half; if larger, in the right half. Each comparison
eliminates half the remaining elements, so a list of one million items needs at most
about twenty comparisons. Binary search requires the list to be sorted in advance.

Sorting arranges a list into order. Bubble sort, a simple teaching algorithm,
repeatedly steps through the list and swaps adjacent elements that are out of order;
it is easy to understand but slow on large lists. Merge sort divides the list in half,
sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves; it is dramatically faster on large
inputs. Efficient sorting matters because sorted data enables fast operations like
binary search.

Computer scientists compare algorithms by how their running time grows with input
size, written in Big-O notation. Linear search is O(n): doubling the list doubles the
worst-case work. Binary search is O(log n): doubling a sorted list adds only one more
comparison. Bubble sort is O(n²), while merge sort is O(n log n). For small inputs the
difference barely matters, but at scale the growth rate dominates everything else.
